y-m-82-01.title: How should we recommend a cheaper plan?
y-m-82-01.topic: Comparing Phone Plans with Linear Expressions
y-m-82-01.goal: When comparing plans with different base fees and per-usage prices, judge 'what more we need to know to make a recommendation,' find usage amounts that meet a condition yourself, and write the evidence and the limits of the recommendation.
y-m-82-01.material:
There are three imaginary plans (the amounts are made up for this task). Data usage is counted in whole 1GB units, and monthly usage is from 0GB to 30GB.
Plan A: base fee 9,000원 + 1,500원 per 1GB.
Plan B: base fee 3,000원 + 2,500원 per 1GB.
Plan C: 24,000원 every month regardless of usage (up to 30GB).
A friend, Minseo (an imaginary person), asked, 'Recommend the cheapest plan for me.'
y-m-82-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is enough
y-m-82-01.thinking.1: Comparing two factors (base fee and unit price) together
y-m-82-01.thinking.2: Finding examples that meet the conditions yourself
y-m-82-01.thinking.3: Saying under what conditions the recommendation would change
y-m-82-01.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H1 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-01.prereq.1: Calculating the linear expression 'base fee + unit price × usage' without letters (middle school level)
y-m-82-01.prereq.2: Multiplying and adding decimals and large numbers, comparing with inequality signs
y-m-82-01.s.s1.prompt: You want to recommend the cheapest plan to Minseo. With only the information known so far, what is the most suitable judgment?
y-m-82-01.s.s1.hint.0: Choose one amount of usage (for example 1GB) and calculate the three fees. Then change the usage a lot (for example 30GB) and calculate again.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the cheapest plan is the same in the two cases.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.o.a: B has the cheapest base fee, so its total is cheapest too, and we can just recommend B.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.r.a: Looking only at the base fee misses the difference in the fee per 1GB that builds up as usage grows.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.o.b: A has the cheapest fee per 1GB, so its total is cheapest too, and we can just recommend A.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.r.b: Looking only at the unit price misses the difference in the base fee you have to pay from the start.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.o.c: Without knowing the usage we can't choose just one, and which plan is cheaper depends on the usage.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.r.c: You noticed that the fee depends on both the base fee and the usage.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.o.d: C is a flat monthly fee, so the fee is the same even if the usage changes, and we can say it is always the cheapest.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.r.d: You missed that a flat fee can be more expensive because you pay the same amount even in months when you use little.
y-m-82-01.s.s1.explain: With 1GB, A is 10,500원, B is 5,500원, and C is 24,000원, so B is cheapest. With 30GB, A is 54,000원, B is 78,000원, and C is 24,000원, so C is cheapest. The cheapest plan changes with the usage, so we need information about the usage. (At 10GB, A and C are equal at 24,000원.)
y-m-82-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different monthly usages x (GB) where 'C is clearly cheaper than both A and B.' If the fees are equal, it is not 'clearly cheaper.'
y-m-82-01.s.s2.hint.0: Change the usage to 8, 9, 10, 11 and compare the fees of A and B each with 24,000원.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.hint.1: You must leave out usages where either plan is 24,000원 or less. Find the smallest usage where both go over 24,000원.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The usage is an integer from 0 to 30.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The usage must be an integer number of GB from 0 to 30.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.ok.c2: At this usage, A is more expensive than C.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.fail.c2: At this usage, A is not more expensive than C.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.ok.c3: At this usage, B is also more expensive than C.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.fail.c3: At this usage, B is not more expensive than C.
y-m-82-01.s.s2.explain: For A, 9,000+1,500x must be greater than 24,000, so x must be greater than 10; for B, 3,000+2,500x must be greater than 24,000, so x must be greater than about 8.4. The integers that satisfy both are 11 to 30. At 10GB, A and C are equal, so it is not 'clearly cheaper.'
y-m-82-01.s.s3.prompt: Minseo's data usage for the last 4 months was 5GB, 9GB, 14GB, and 7GB. Assume it stays similar in the future and recommend one plan. Give at least one number as your evidence, and write one condition under which the recommendation could change.
y-m-82-01.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate each plan for each month and make a table (5, 9, 14, 7GB).
y-m-82-01.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the 4-month totals or the lowest for each month, and see which month changes the result.
y-m-82-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Can the evidence for the plan you recommended be checked with the numbers you gave?
y-m-82-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is the condition under which the recommendation changes connected to usage?
y-m-82-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you separate what you can say from the 4 months of data and what you can't?
y-m-82-01.s.s3.model.0: The 4-month totals are 88,500원 for A, 99,500원 for B, and 96,000원 for C, so I recommend A. But if months like 14GB come often, C could be better, so if usage goes up a lot in the future, we should compare again.
y-m-82-01.s.s3.model.1: Month by month, B (15,500원) is cheapest at 5GB and C (24,000원) is cheapest at 14GB, so it differs by month. If we pick only one plan, I think A, which has the lowest total, is better, but we can't be sure about the future from only 4 months of data.

y-m-82-02.title: Can we trust a rule for the number of regions as points are added?
y-m-82-02.topic: Inductive Guesses and Counterexamples (Points and Regions on a Circle)
y-m-82-02.goal: Experience how a rule made from the first few data points is tested by new data, and say what evidence and next actions are needed to 'confirm' a rule.
y-m-82-02.material:
Put n points on a circle and join every pair of points with a line segment. Choose the points so that no three segments meet at one point (for example, the diagonals of a regular hexagon do not qualify, since three meet at the center). Let R(n) be the number of regions these segments divide the inside of the circle into.
For those who can't see a picture, here is a description in words. When n=3, one triangle forms, with 1 region inside the triangle and 3 regions outside the triangle, so R(3)=4.
y-m-82-02.thinking.1: Revising or keeping your judgment with new information
y-m-82-02.thinking.2: Judging the power of a counterexample
y-m-82-02.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H1 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-02.prereq.1: Experience finding the rule of a sequence and saying the next term (middle school level)
y-m-82-02.prereq.2: Joining points on a circle with segments and counting regions (it is enough if you can draw it yourself or read the table below)
y-m-82-02.s.s1.prompt: Watch how your judgment changes each time the data grows.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write R(n) and 2^(n−1) side by side in a table.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.hint.1: At each step, separate 'what I can say from the data now' and 'what I don't know yet.'
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Drawing and counting directly gives R(1)=1, R(2)=2, R(3)=4, R(4)=8.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is R(5)? Choose the most reasonable judgment with the data you have now.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Different judgments like a, b, and c can all be reasonable. See which guess remains with the next data.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 16 : The number has kept doubling, so the next will double too.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a judgment that sets up one candidate rule. It is good to remember that it is a guess from 4 data points.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 15 : The amount added will be 7 after 1, 2, 4.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that sets up a different candidate rule. When there is little data, different rules can all look correct.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: With only 4 data points, it is hard to settle on a single R(5).
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a judgment to put off deciding when there is little data.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: R(5) is less than R(4)=8. When points increase, regions decrease.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This does not fit the observation that more points mean more segments and the regions are divided more.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Drawing R(5) exactly and counting gives 16. Now it is 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you judge R(6)? Choose the one that fits your judgment now.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.after: It is reasonable to think it is 32, and also reasonable to put off being sure. But 5 examples do not guarantee every n.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: R(6)=32. It has doubled five times in a row.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is a judgment that makes a prediction that matches the data so far. It is still a guess before counting directly.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It will probably be close to 32, but we can't be sure until we count directly.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This is a judgment that even when the data grows, the general rule has to be checked separately.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: R(6)=30. The regions will increase a little less than doubling.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You decided a value that does not come from the data, without evidence.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: R(6)=48. From now on it will triple each time.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: There is nothing in the data to suggest that the rule suddenly changes.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Drawing R(6) exactly and counting gives 31 (the points were chosen so that no three segments meet at one point). By the same method, R(7)=57.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is your judgment now about the rule 'R(n)=2^(n−1)'?
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.after: 2^(n−1) meets a counterexample at n=6, where the value is 31. One counterexample is enough. (In fact, it is known that R(n)=1+n(n−1)/2+n(n−1)(n−2)(n−3)/24.)
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is still correct. The 31 came from counting the regions wrong or drawing the picture wrong.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a judgment that throws away data that does not fit, without evidence. If the value was counted following the conditions, there is no reason to discard it.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It failed at R(6), so we can't say it holds for every n. The 5 examples were not enough evidence.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This is a judgment that uses the fact that one counterexample breaks a general rule.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If we change the rule to R(n)=2^(n−1)−1, it will be right all the way to R(6).
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that only changed the formula to fit R(6). It already fails for R(1)=1 and R(2)=2.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: This rule is broken. We don't know the correct rule, but we should test new candidates, including R(7)=57.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment to discard the broken rule and test new candidates with more data.
y-m-82-02.s.s1.reflect: If you first chose a or b, find the part that changed as the data grew. If you first chose c (putting off deciding), notice that this judgment could have stayed the same to the end. Check whether at every step you separated 'what I can say from the data seen so far' and 'what I don't know yet.'
y-m-82-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose the lines in Jion's (an imaginary person) argument that lack evidence or are wrong.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.hint.0: Sort each line into 'what was seen,' 'a guess,' or 'a conclusion.'
y-m-82-02.s.s2.hint.1: Compare whether the conclusion line is justified by the earlier lines alone, and what check is missing.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.line.0: 1) When there are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 points, the regions are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.line.1: 2) It doubled five times in a row, so it can't be chance.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.line.2: 3) Therefore with 6 points the regions will also be 32.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.line.3: 4) I drew it with 6 points and counted 31, but I must have drawn the picture wrong.
y-m-82-02.s.s2.explain: Line 2 was sure it 'can't be chance' from only 5 examples. Line 4 threw away data that does not fit the rule without evidence, and line 5 declares it 'certain' as a result of that. Line 1 is an observation, and line 3 is fine as a guess.
y-m-82-02.s.s3.prompt: Write what evidence you would need to confirm 'R(n)=2^(n−1)' as the rule, and two things you would do next after R(6)=31 came out.
y-m-82-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write the most reliable fact among the values you have seen so far.
y-m-82-02.s.s3.hint.1: To confirm a rule, think about what you need, not 'checking a few more cases.'
y-m-82-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Because ..., I will try to ...
y-m-82-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what effect R(6)=31 has on the rule?
y-m-82-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say the evidence needed to trust the rule (a reason, not the number of examples)?
y-m-82-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is your next action concrete (for example, drawing 7 points, or testing a new candidate)?
y-m-82-02.s.s3.model.0: R(6)=31, which differs from 2^(n−1)=32, so this rule is broken. To trust a rule, I need to be able to explain (prove) why it holds for every n, rather than just collect more examples. Next I will count with 7 points and look for another rule that fits 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31.
y-m-82-02.s.s3.model.1: One counterexample (n=6, 31 regions) has come out, so we can't confirm this rule. I think I could explain a rule by collecting more examples and working out why adding one more point increases the regions by that many.

y-m-82-03.title: If you use a wall, is a square the largest?
y-m-82-03.topic: Area Modeled with a Quadratic Expression (A Fence That Uses a Wall)
y-m-82-03.goal: Check whether the familiar conclusion 'a square is the largest' still holds when the conditions change and find the error, make several designs within the constraints, and then explain how the best design changes when the conditions change.
y-m-82-03.material: You want to build a rectangular chicken coop with 40 m of fence. If you put one side against a straight wall (25 m long), that side needs no fence. Let the length of the side parallel to the wall be a m, and the length of each of the two sides perpendicular to the wall be b m. All 40 m of fence is used, so a+2b=40, and the wall is only 25 m, so a cannot be more than 25 m. The unit of length is m, and the unit of area is m².
y-m-82-03.thinking.0: Finding the error of carrying a conclusion over to a situation with different conditions
y-m-82-03.thinking.2: Predicting the best design as conditions change
y-m-82-03.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H1 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-03.prereq.1: Understanding the shape of the graph of the quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c (a parabola that opens downward is largest at its vertex)
y-m-82-03.prereq.2: Removing one variable from a relationship between two variables to write it as an expression in one variable (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-82-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line with the error in Haeun's (an imaginary person) solution.
y-m-82-03.s.s1.hint.0: Directly calculate and compare the area of the design with a=b and the designs with b changed to 10, 12, and 8.
y-m-82-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare what conditions each line's fact was learned under and whether they are the same as the conditions now.
y-m-82-03.s.s1.line.0: 1) The area is S=a×b and a+2b=40, so a=40−2b and S=b(40−2b).
y-m-82-03.s.s1.line.1: 2) I learned that for a rectangle with a fixed perimeter and no wall, the area is largest when it is a square.
y-m-82-03.s.s1.line.2: 3) So if we set a=b, then 40−2b=b, that is, a=b=40/3.
y-m-82-03.s.s1.line.4: 5) Therefore the largest area of this chicken coop is about 177.8 m².
y-m-82-03.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the error. 'A square is the largest' is the result for when the fence is used on all four sides, but here, because of the wall, the fence is used on only three sides, so the conditions are different. In fact, with b=10 and a=20 (25 or less), S=200, which is bigger than 177.8, so the 'largest' in line 5 is wrong too.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different designs where a and b are both natural numbers (m) and the area is 180 m² or more. Use all 40 m of the fence, and a cannot be more than 25 m.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.hint.0: Once you choose b, a is decided, so change b one at a time and organize a and the area in a table.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.hint.1: Find the designs that are ruled out by the wall length condition and the designs that are ruled out by the area condition.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.var.a: Side parallel to the wall, a (m)
y-m-82-03.s.s2.var.b: Side perpendicular to the wall, b (m)
y-m-82-03.s.s2.ok.c1: a and b are natural numbers.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be natural numbers.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.ok.c2: You used all 40 m of the fence.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.ok.c3: It fits within the wall length.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.fail.c3: a is more than the wall length of 25 m.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The area is 180 m² or more.
y-m-82-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The area is less than 180 m².
y-m-82-03.s.s2.explain: The designs that satisfy the conditions are (a,b)=(24,8), (22,9), (20,10), (18,11), (16,12), (14,13), with areas 192, 198, 200, 198, 192, 182. With a=26 it goes over the wall, and with a=30 the area is 150, which is not enough.
y-m-82-03.s.s3.prompt: If the wall is only 15 m long instead of 25 m (a is 15 m or less), will the largest design be the same as before, or different? Write your reason using numbers.
y-m-82-03.s.s3.hint.0: First check whether the original best design a=20 satisfies the new condition (a≤15).
y-m-82-03.s.s3.hint.1: Change b to 12, 12.5, 13 and calculate a and the area to compare.
y-m-82-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: It is the same / It changes. Because ...
y-m-82-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the original best (a=20, b=10) can be used under the new condition?
y-m-82-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you give the best design under the new condition with numbers?
y-m-82-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is your reason connected to the way the area grows and then shrinks as b changes?
y-m-82-03.s.s3.model.0: It changes. Originally a=20, b=10 (area 200) was the largest, but if the wall is 15 m, a=20 can't be used. The area is largest at b=10 and gets smaller as you move away from it, so in the possible range (b≥12.5), using b=12.5 and a=15 gives an area of 187.5.
y-m-82-03.s.s3.model.1: I think it changes. If a is 15 or less and can only be made from even natural numbers, a=14, b=13 (area 182) is the largest design. With a=15, b=12.5, which is not a natural number. It is smaller than the original maximum of 200.

y-m-82-04.title: The success rate is lower, yet it is more accurate?
y-m-82-04.topic: Comparing Ratios and Differences in Makeup (Whole and Parts)
y-m-82-04.goal: When the overall ratio and the ratios by condition tell different stories, judge what must be made the same for a fair comparison, and make such data yourself.
y-m-82-04.material: Two imaginary students, 가 and 나, each practiced basketball shots 100 times. They threw from a place close to the hoop (near) and a place far from it (far), and the shooting success rate is the number of successes ÷ the number of throws. The practice followed the same rules, and the students chose the places and the number of throws.
y-m-82-04.thinking.0: Revising or keeping your judgment with new information
y-m-82-04.thinking.1: Checking whether the conditions of a comparison are controlled
y-m-82-04.thinking.2: Making data that fits the conditions
y-m-82-04.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H1 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-04.prereq.1: Finding and comparing ratios with fractions and percentages (successes ÷ attempts)
y-m-82-04.prereq.2: Comparing the sizes of two fractions (common denominators or converting to percentages)
y-m-82-04.s.s1.prompt: Watch how your judgment about 'who is more accurate' changes each time there is more information.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.hint.0: Make a table of the ratio of successes at each place divided by the number of throws.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the number of throws from each place is the same or different for 가 and 나.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.info: After 100 throws each, 가 made 50 and 나 made 74.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Who do you judge to be the more accurate shooter?
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.after: A judgment that looks only at the number of successes and a judgment that we need to know more about where they threw from are both reasonable for now.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 나 is more accurate. 74 is more than 50.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment compares by the number of successes. Since the number of throws is the same, it is natural with the information now.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: 가 is more accurate. The number of successes is smaller.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read it as the one with fewer successes being better. You read the meaning of the numbers backwards.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is hard to say for sure with only this information. We don't know where they threw from.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment looks at the conditions of the comparison (the place thrown from), not just the number of successes.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Their accuracy is the same. They each threw 100 times.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You said the number of throws is the same and ignored the difference in the number of successes.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Here are the records by place thrown from. 가: 18 successes out of 20 near, 32 successes out of 80 far. 나: 68 successes out of 80 near, 6 successes out of 20 far.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: What story comes out when you compare by place?
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.after: 가: near 90%, far 40%. 나: near 85%, far 30%. Comparing the same places, 가 is higher in both.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 가's success rate is higher both near and far.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You compared with successes ÷ throws at each place.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 나 made more successes near the hoop, so 나 is more accurate.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You compared the number of successes directly in two cases where the number of throws is different.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 나's total is bigger, so my first judgment stays the same.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You did not take into account that the records by place show something that was hidden by the totals.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: 나 is more accurate near, and 가 is more accurate far.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You mixed up counts and ratios, and compared the near ratios backwards.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Of the 100 throws, 80 of 가's were far, and 80 of 나's were near.
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Then what is your judgment now about 'who is the more accurate shooter'?
y-m-82-04.s.s1.st.2.after: Depending on what the question means, a, b, and c all make sense. d goes too far, because it claims 'in every case' from just two records.

y-m-82-05.title: If a statement is true for three numbers, is it true for four?
y-m-82-05.topic: Sums of Consecutive Numbers Seen Through Odd and Even
y-m-82-05.goal: Before generalizing a rule checked with a few examples, investigate in which cases it holds by using counterexamples and reasons.
y-m-82-05.material: Doyun (an imaginary person) did some calculations. 1+2+3=6, 4+5+6=15, and 10+11+12=33 are all multiples of 3. So Doyun said, 'The sum of k consecutive natural numbers is always a multiple of k.' (k is an integer 2 or more.)
y-m-82-05.thinking.0: Evaluating how far the evidence from examples goes
y-m-82-05.thinking.2: Finding the condition under which it holds and explaining the reason
y-m-82-05.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H1 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-05.prereq.1: The meaning of odd and even numbers and multiples

y-m-82-05.prereq.3: Checking whether the remainder is 0 or not
y-m-82-05.s.s1.prompt: What does it tell you about Doyun's statement ('the sum of k consecutive numbers is always a multiple of k') that 1+2+3, 4+5+6, and 10+11+12 were all multiples of 3?
y-m-82-05.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many values of k Doyun tested.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate a few cases that were not tested directly, like k=4 and 5, and check whether the claim is true.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.o.a: It was right three times, so we can say that whatever k is, the sum is a multiple of k.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.r.a: You extended the checking for k=3 to other k.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.o.b: It is only evidence for k=3, not a proof, and it tells us nothing about other k.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.r.b: This judgment separates the range the examples speak for (k=3, the three cases checked).
y-m-82-05.s.s1.o.c: All three examples were right, so for k=3 the proof is already finished.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.r.c: You treated checking a few examples as the same as explaining every case.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.o.d: There are only three examples, so they tell us nothing even about the case k=3.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.r.d: This judgment takes too low a view of the fact that examples count as evidence.
y-m-82-05.s.s1.explain: The three examples support the claim for k=3 but are not a proof. Also, other cases like k=4 were never tested.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 counterexamples, with different k, where the sum is not a multiple of k. k is an integer from 2 to 12, and the first number n is a natural number from 1 to 50. (The sum of k consecutive natural numbers starting from n)
y-m-82-05.s.s2.hint.0: Starting from small counts like k=2, 4, 6, change the first number and add directly.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.hint.1: Collect in a table which k give counterexamples easily.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.ok.c1: k and n are integers within the range.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.fail.c1: k must be an integer from 2 to 12, and n an integer from 1 to 50.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum is not a multiple of k. It is a counterexample.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.fail.c2: In this case the sum is a multiple of k. It is not a counterexample.
y-m-82-05.s.s2.explain: With k=4, n=1, 1+2+3+4=10 is not a multiple of 4. With k=6, n=3, 3+4+5+6+7+8=33 is also not a multiple of 6. With k=3, n=5, 5+6+7=18, and with k=5, n=2, 2+3+4+5+6=20, so both are multiples.
y-m-82-05.s.s3.prompt: Write the rule for which k the sum of k consecutive numbers is a multiple of k and for which k it is not, and the reason. You may use examples or expressions with letters.
y-m-82-05.s.s3.hint.0: For k=3, 5, 7, write the sum in terms of the middle number and the count.
y-m-82-05.s.s3.hint.1: For k=2, 4, 6, compare what form the sum divided by the count (the average) takes.
y-m-82-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: When k is ..., it is ... Because ...
y-m-82-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly state the rule (for which k it holds)?
y-m-82-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is your reason an explanation that works for every case, not just one example?
y-m-82-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can your explanation predict a new k (for example 7 or 8)?
y-m-82-05.s.s3.model.0: When k is odd, there is a middle number, so the sum is (middle number)×k, which is a multiple of k. When k is even, there is no middle number and the average is a decimal (x.5), so the sum is not a multiple of k. For example, 1+2+3+4=10 is not a multiple of 4.
y-m-82-05.s.s3.model.1: The sum can be written as k×n+k(k−1)/2. The first part, k×n, is always a multiple of k, so the question is whether the second part, k(k−1)/2, is a multiple of k. Only when (k−1) is even, that is, when k is odd, is this value an integer multiple of k, so it holds only for odd k.

y-m-82-07.title: Can we talk about the slope at a corner?
y-m-82-07.topic: Existence of the Derivative and Left and Right Limits
y-m-82-07.goal: Instead of a first impression about symmetry or shape, judge whether a derivative exists by how the left and right average rates of change behave, and apply this judgment to several functions.
y-m-82-07.material: The function f(x)=|x| is x when x is 0 or more, and −x when x is less than 0 (read as: f of x is the absolute value of x). Find out whether there is a derivative at x=0. The average rate of change is (f(0+h)−f(0))/h (h is a nonzero number), and if it gets close to one value as h gets closer and closer to 0, that value is the derivative. Look separately at the side where h is positive (right) and the side where h is negative (left).
y-m-82-07.thinking.0: Testing a first impression (symmetry) with data
y-m-82-07.thinking.1: Judging a limit by splitting into left and right
y-m-82-07.thinking.2: Evaluating the limits of the 'shape' heuristic
y-m-82-07.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H2 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-07.prereq.1: The meaning of the average rate of change (f(a+h)−f(a))/h
y-m-82-07.prereq.2: The definition of the derivative (if the average rate of change gets close to one value as h→0, that value) and the meaning of the left limit and right limit (introductory calculus level; derivative formulas are not needed)
y-m-82-07.prereq.3: The meaning of the absolute value function |x|
y-m-82-07.s.s1.prompt: Watch how your judgment about the derivative at x=0 changes each time new information comes out.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.hint.0: Split h into positive and negative, calculate the average rate of change separately, and write it in a table.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.hint.1: Compare what number each side gets close to and whether the two sides are the same.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.info: The graph of f(x)=|x| is the same on the left and right of the y-axis, and it is a 'V' shape with a sharp corner at the origin.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think the derivative at x=0 will be?
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.after: Right now both a (a guess based on symmetry) and c (putting off deciding and looking at left and right separately) make sense. Now let's observe the values directly.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is 0. The left and right are symmetric, so the slope will be 0 too.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This judgment guesses the slope from the first impression of symmetry. We need to check whether it holds at a corner too.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is 1, because to the right of the origin y=x.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment was made by looking at only the right side.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It's hard to settle on one. We need to look at the right and the left separately.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment points out that approaching from the left and right must be looked at separately.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: It is −1, because to the left of the origin y=−x.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This judgment was made by looking at only the left side.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.ask: What does this observation tell you about your first judgment?
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.after: The left limit is −1 and the right limit is 1, so the limit is not settled as a single value. So f(x)=|x| has no derivative at x=0. The guess that it is 0 because of symmetry was not right.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It gets close to 1 on the right and −1 on the left, so it is not settled as a single value.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This judgment compared the left and right values separately.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The average of the right value 1 and the left value −1, which is 0, is the derivative.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You averaged the left and right values into one value. The derivative must be the one value that the average rate of change gets close to.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The value stays constant as h gets smaller, so the derivative is 1.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You used only the observation on the right and ignored the observation on the left.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Whichever side h comes from, it gets close to −1, so the derivative is −1.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You used only the observation on the left and ignored the observation on the right.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.info: This time it is g(x)=x|x| (x² when x is 0 or more, −x² when x is less than 0). Its graph passes smoothly through the origin. When h=0.1, 0.01, 0.001, (g(h)−g(0))/h is 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and when h=−0.1, −0.01, −0.001, it is also 0.1, 0.01, 0.001.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is your judgment about the derivative of g(x)=x|x| at x=0?
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.after: The average rate of change of g equals the size of h, so it gets close to 0 on both sides. So g has a derivative of 0 at x=0. Having an absolute value in it does not always mean there is no derivative.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is 0. The average rate of change gets close to 0 from both the right and the left.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment checked whether the left and right average rates of change get close to the same value.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: There is none. It has an absolute value, so it has a corner like |x|.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged by the impression that the expression has an absolute value. You did not check how the average rate of change actually behaves.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: There is none. It approaches with positive values from the right and negative values from the left.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You misread the observed values. On both sides it gets close to 0 from positive values.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is 0.1. The first value that came out is the derivative.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You mistook the value at one particular h for the derivative. You need the value as h is sent close to 0.
y-m-82-07.s.s1.reflect: If you first chose a (0), look at which observation about |x| changed that judgment, and if you first chose c, look at whether your judgment continued to the end. Organize the point that you judge by how the left and right average rates of change behave, not by symmetry or the look of the expression alone.
y-m-82-07.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the functions below that have a derivative at x=0. (How to read: ㄱ is x squared, ㄴ is the absolute value of x plus x, ㄷ is x times the absolute value of x, ㄹ is the absolute value of x plus x squared, ㅁ is the cube of the absolute value of x)

y-m-82-07.s.s2.explain: For a, c, and e, the average rates of change on the right and the left get close to the same value (0), so there is a derivative. For b, it is 2 on the right and 0 on the left, and for d, it is 1 on the right and −1 on the left, so there is none.
y-m-82-07.s.s3.prompt: Is the statement 'if the graph looks sharp there is no derivative, and if it looks smooth there is one' reliable? Evaluate it by giving at least one function you saw in this task as an example.
y-m-82-07.s.s3.hint.0: Compare and write the values of the right and left average rates of change for |x| and for x|x|.

y-m-82-08.title: If it worked ten times, will it keep being prime?
y-m-82-08.topic: An Expression That Looks Like a Rule, and Searching for Counterexamples
y-m-82-08.goal: Test the generalization of an expression that seems to hold for several values by searching for counterexamples, and explain with evidence that checking and proving are different.

y-m-82-10.title: If the middle is high, will a truck pass through?
y-m-82-10.topic: Reading the Conditions of a Quadratic Model (A Tunnel Cross Section)
y-m-82-10.goal: Find the error of judging from the value at a single point, make several designs that meet the conditions in a quadratic model, and explain the limits of the assumptions.
y-m-82-10.material: Think about the cross section of a parabola-shaped tunnel (unit of length: m). The floor is y=0, and the width of the floor is 12 m (from x=−6 to x=6). If the height at the center (x=0) is h m, the upper line on the inside of the tunnel is y=h−(h/36)x² (y=0 at x=±6). The vehicle passing through is 4 m high, and its outer side can come as far as 4.5 m from the center of the tunnel (x=4.5 or x=−4.5). For safety, you must leave 0.5 m of clearance above the vehicle.

y-m-82-10.s.s1.prompt: This is Hyeonu's (an imaginary person) notice about a tunnel with a center height of 10 m (h=10). Choose the lines that lack enough evidence to guarantee safety.

y-m-82-10.s.s1.hint.1: Compare that height with the required height of 4.5 m.
y-m-82-10.s.s1.line.0: 1) The upper line is y=10−(10/36)x² (x is the horizontal distance from the center of the tunnel, in m).
y-m-82-10.s.s1.line.1: 2) The vehicle's height is 4 m, and adding the 0.5 m clearance gives 4.5 m.
y-m-82-10.s.s1.line.2: 3) The upper line is highest at the center, so we just compare the center height of 10 m with 4.5 m.
y-m-82-10.s.s1.line.3: 4) 10>4.5, so the central part is high enough.
y-m-82-10.s.s1.line.4: 5) Therefore the vehicle can pass even if its outer side is 4.5 m from the center.
y-m-82-10.s.s1.explain: Lines 3 and 5 are the problem. The upper line is highest at the center, so comparing only the height at the center does not check the height where the vehicle really is. At x=4.5, where the outer side of the vehicle is, the height of the upper line is 10−(10/36)×4.5²≈4.375 m, which is lower than the required 4.5 m.

y-m-82-11.title: Among thirty people, will there be a pair with the same birthday?
y-m-82-11.topic: Estimating Probability and the Model's Assumptions (Same Birthday)
y-m-82-11.goal: Test with a calculation the intuition for estimating a probability when there are many pairs, and explain why the sum of events does not give the probability and how the model's assumptions affect the result.
y-m-82-11.material: There are 30 students in a class (an imaginary class). Count a year as 365 days (leaving out births on February 29), and assume that everyone is equally likely to be born on any day and that they do not affect each other. Find out 'the probability that there is at least one pair of students born on the same day.'
y-m-82-11.thinking.1: Revising a judgment with new information
y-m-82-11.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H2 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-11.prereq.1: The meaning of counting cases and probability, the multiplication rule (independent events), and the probability of the complement (1−P)
y-m-82-11.prereq.2: Knowing the number of pairs when choosing two from n people (combinations): 435 pairs for 30 people
y-m-82-11.s.s1.prompt: Watch how your estimate changes each time there is more information.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write the value you estimate using the number of pairs, 435, and the probability of one pair, 1/365.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.hint.1: If your estimate goes over 1 (100%), think about what the reason could be.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.info: The number of pairs made by choosing two different people from 30 is 435. The probability that one particular pair was born on the same day is 1/365.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you estimate 'the probability that there is at least one pair born on the same day'?
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.after: There are many pairs, so the probability can be quite large, but adding the probabilities of the pairs one by one counts overlaps twice, so the exact value has to be calculated separately.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 435/365 is bigger than 1, so there must be one. The probability is 100%.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You added probabilities while ignoring that the events overlap.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.o.b: There are many pairs, so it is much bigger than 1/365, but we can't say it is 100%.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This judgment looked at both the fact that there are many pairs and the problem of counting overlaps.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.o.c: One pair is 1/365, so even with 30 people it stays at about 1 to 2%.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You missed that there are as many as 435 pairs.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There are 30 people and a year has 365 days, so it is 30/365, about 8%.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You mixed up the number of people, 30, with the number of pairs.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.o.e: It is hard to estimate with only this information. You have to calculate the overlapping cases separately.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.0.r.e: This judgment puts off estimating and points out the calculation that is needed.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.info: The probability that 'no one shares a day' is found by multiplying in order: 365/365 × 364/365 × 363/365 × … × 336/365 ≈ 0.294.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.ask: Then what is the probability that there is at least one pair born on the same day?
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.after: 1−0.294≈0.706, so about 71%. The first estimate that there must be one was too much, and the estimate of 1 to 2% was too small.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You answered with the probability that 'no one overlaps' as it is.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This judgment used the idea of the complement: subtract the probability of no overlap from the whole, 1.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the value of one pair's probability, 1/365, used as it is.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You used the number of people divided by 365.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.info: If you change the number of people, the probability that there is a pair born on the same day is about 12% for 10 people, about 51% for 23 people, and about 89% for 40 people. This calculation assumes that 'the probability of birth on every day is the same' and 'the students do not affect each other.'
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which of these assumptions could change the result the most in reality?
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.after: Both a and b are assumptions that can change the result. c has a very small effect, and d is a condition, not an assumption.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is the assumption that the probability of birth on every day is the same. The actual number of births differs from day to day.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This judgment pointed out concretely how the assumption could differ from reality.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It is the assumption that the students do not affect each other. Twins can be in the same class.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This judgment pointed out that the assumption of independence can be broken by how classes are formed.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is the assumption that no student was born on February 29.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The difference between 365 days and 366 days is very small, so it does not change the result much.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is the number of people itself, 30 students.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.st.2.r.d: It is a given condition, not an assumption.
y-m-82-11.s.s1.reflect: If you first chose b or e, look at how the calculation result carried your judgment forward, and if you first chose a, c, or d, look at what changed your judgment. Organize how intuition, calculation, and checking assumptions complement each other.
y-m-82-11.s.s2.prompt: A friend calculated, '435 pairs × (1/365) = about 1.19, that is 119%, so there must be a pair born on the same day.' Explain why this calculation is wrong, and write what kind of number 1.19 could be.
y-m-82-11.s.s2.hint.0: Give an example where two pairs can have the same birthday at the same time.
y-m-82-11.s.s2.hint.1: Recall the range of values a probability can take and compare it with the calculation result.
y-m-82-11.s.s2.placeholder: Example: This calculation is wrong because ...
y-m-82-11.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say why adding probabilities pair by pair counts overlaps?
y-m-82-11.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain 1.19 as something other than a 'probability,' such as an 'average count'?
y-m-82-11.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say why the word 'must' goes too far?
y-m-82-11.s.s2.model.0: If you add the probabilities pair by pair, the case where two pairs share a birthday at the same time is counted several times, so they overlap. So the sum can go over 100%, like 119%, but a probability cannot go over 100%, so it is a wrong calculation. 1.19 can be seen as something like the average number of pairs born on the same day.
y-m-82-11.s.s2.model.1: The events for each pair overlap, so you can't just add the probabilities. 1.19 only means that there are about 1.19 pairs born on the same day on average, not that there must be one. There can be quite a few classes with not a single pair.

y-m-82-12.s.s1.hint.0: For r equal to 1, 2, 5, 10, find h so that the volume is 500, calculate the surface area, and compare.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.hint.1: Observe what happens to the surface area when r is very small and when r is very large.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.o.a: A thin, long shape uses the least, because the top and bottom circles become small.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.r.a: You looked only at the advantage of the circles getting smaller and missed that the side gets bigger.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.o.b: A flat shape uses the least, because the height is low and the side becomes small.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the advantage of the side getting smaller and missed that the top and bottom get bigger.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.o.c: Somewhere in the middle, neither too thin nor too flat, uses the least.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.r.c: This judgment saw that the shapes at both ends could be disadvantageous.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.o.d: If the volume is the same, any shape will have the same surface area.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.r.d: You thought that the condition of equal volume makes the surface area equal too.
y-m-82-12.s.s1.explain: When r is very small, the side gets long, and when r is very large, the top and bottom get big, so the surface area is large at both ends. So it is likely to get smaller somewhere in between. Let's actually try it and check.

y-m-82-13.title: How far can a quick estimation method be trusted?
y-m-82-13.topic: The Range of an Estimation Rule (Years to Double)
y-m-82-13.goal: Test whether an estimation method that works for a few interest rates works for all interest rates, find the cases where it fails yourself, and explain with evidence the range in which it can be trusted.
y-m-82-13.material: There is an estimation method that says if you save with compound interest at an annual rate of r% (interest is added to the principal every year), it takes about 72÷r years for the principal to double. When the number of years 72/r found by this method has passed, the multiple of the principal can be calculated as (1+r/100)^(72/r) (decimal numbers of years are calculated by the same expression). If this multiple is close to 2, the estimation method works well. Jinseo (an imaginary person) saw that for r=6, 1.06^12≈2.012, and for r=8, 1.08^9≈1.999, and said, 'It works well whatever the interest rate is.' (This is an imaginary situation and has nothing to do with real products.)
y-m-82-13.thinking.0: Evaluating how far the evidence for a generalization goes
y-m-82-13.thinking.1: Searching for counterexamples (cases that don't fit)
y-m-82-13.thinking.2: Deciding the range where the estimation method applies
y-m-82-13.prereq.0: School order assumption: this task's H2 is only a difficulty level for high school math inquiry activities, and it does not mean the task is assigned to any particular grade.
y-m-82-13.prereq.1: Compound interest: a principal of 1 at an annual rate of r% for n years becomes (1+r/100)^n times
y-m-82-13.prereq.2: Can calculate decimal exponents (for example 1.4^1.8) with a calculator
y-m-82-13.s.s1.prompt: What do Jinseo's two cases (r=6, r=8) tell you about the statement 'it works well whatever the interest rate is'?
y-m-82-13.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate (1+r/100)^(72/r) for rates that are far apart, such as r=1, 4, 20, 50.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.hint.1: Compare how far each is from 2 with the cases of 6% and 8%.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.o.a: Both rates are very close to 2, so we can say it works for all rates.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.r.a: You extended the agreement of two cases to all interest rates.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.o.b: The errors are 0.012 and 0.001, so this estimation method is useless.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.r.b: You took a small error as too big. An estimation method is still useful even with a little error.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.o.c: We can say it is a method that gets more and more accurate the higher the rate is.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.r.c: You decided the direction of change from just two cases. It is a claim that was never actually checked.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.o.d: It is only evidence that it works near the two rates, and rates farther away must be tested separately.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.r.d: This judgment separates the range that was checked from the range that was not.
y-m-82-13.s.s1.explain: The two cases are only evidence that the method works well near 6 to 8%. Rates far away, like 1% or 50%, have to be calculated separately.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.prompt: Look for rates at which the method is off a lot. Enter 3 different integer rates r (%), from 1 to 100, for which (1+r/100)^(72/r) is off from 2 by 0.15 or more.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.hint.0: Spread the rates far apart, like 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, and calculate (1+r/100)^(72/r).
y-m-82-13.s.s2.hint.1: Compare in a table whether the amount it is off from 2 gets bigger or smaller depending on the rate.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.ok.c1: r is an integer from 1 to 100.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.fail.c1: r must be an integer from 1 to 100.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.ok.c2: It is off from 2 by 0.15 or more. The method is off a lot.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.fail.c2: It is off from 2 by less than 0.15. The method works relatively well.
y-m-82-13.s.s2.explain: From r=36 and up, it is off from 2 by 0.15 or more. For r=40, 1.4^1.8≈1.83; for r=50, 1.5^1.44≈1.79; for r=60, it is about 1.76. On the other hand, for r=4 to 12 it fits within 0.03 of 2.
y-m-82-13.s.s3.prompt: Using the numbers you calculated as evidence, write why the rule of 72 is used and the range of rates in which it can be trusted.
y-m-82-13.s.s3.hint.0: Write how far from 2 it is for rates 4, 8, 20, 40, and see from which rate the difference gets large.
y-m-82-13.s.s3.hint.1: Test the range you decided again with one more rate.
y-m-82-13.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the numbers you gave (the multiple or the error) real calculated values?
y-m-82-13.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart the rates where the method works well and the rates where it is off a lot?
y-m-82-13.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you mention both the 'advantage (quick estimating)' and the 'limit'?
y-m-82-13.s.s3.model.0: At a high rate (for example 40%), 1.4^1.8≈1.83 is quite far from 2, but near 6 to 10% it is nearly exact. So use it for quick estimates, but when the rate goes over 20 to 30%, you need an exact calculation.
y-m-82-13.s.s3.model.1: The rule of 72 has the advantage of being easy to do in your head, and even when the rate is low (1 to 2%), the error is within 0.05. But at a high rate like 50%, it gives a value that is not doubled (about 1.79 times), so it is hard to trust. You must first check the range where you use it.
